questions.q: Do we ship at the measured pace, go full time, or bring in a contractor?
questions.lede: One author touched every commit in 90 days; 24 weeks of appetite is 99 to 129 calendar weeks at the measured rate.

rows.label: Calendar length for 24 weeks of appetite
cells: 99 to 129 weeks, at 1.21 commits a week

rows.label: Which phases run now
cells: 0, A, B, D, H; E, F, G move to Later
A and B run alongside D

rows.label: Who ships D and F
cells: A contractor, if pace has not doubled

visual.note: One author touched every commit in the last 90 days.
visual.caption: Three ways to spend the same 24 weeks of appetite.

questions.stakes: Every date in the plan, and whether E, F and G survive as Later, depends on this one answer.
state: 10 distinct commit days in the last 58 days, 1.21 a week.
Since 1 September, 3 commits touched code and 111 touched documents.
One author on every commit in the last 90 days.
tension: The plan's 24-week appetite assumes a pace nobody has measured against it yet.
A contractor moves the pilot forward by about eight weeks, at a cost the plan has not priced.

options.label: Ship at the measured pace, publish dates every Friday
gains: Dates match what is actually happening.
costs: Phases E, F and G move to Later.

options.label: Both founders go full time
gains: The phase table stands as written.
costs: Needs income to cover both, unpriced here.

options.label: Engage a contractor for phases D and F
gains: Phases A and B run alongside D.
The pilot comes forward about eight weeks.
costs: A contractor's cost is not yet quoted.
options.money: A contractor's fee, not yet quoted.

recCase: The measured pace is the only one with evidence behind it.
Dates published every Friday keep the promise honest either way.
questions.flip: Two full months of commits at double today's rate would justify the full-time table without a contractor.
sources: git log on this repository, read 17 September 2026

questions.q: Does Pro's ₹299 price stay, and which model runs the edits and the blueprints?
questions.lede: Sonnet 5 for everything costs ₹321 to ₹367 a Pro month against ₹246 net of tax and the payment fee.

rows.label: Net cost per Pro user a month

visual.note: ₹246.33 is ₹299 net of 18% GST and Razorpay's fee.
visual.caption: Three ways to close the gap between ₹299 and the model bill.

questions.stakes: Every Pro user either earns the studio about ₹60 or costs it about ₹120, on one routing choice.
state: At the caps, Sonnet 5 for everything costs ₹321.47 on the eleven-file blueprint, ₹367 on the fourteen-file one.
₹299 nets ₹246.33 after 18% GST and Razorpay's 2.36% fee.
Haiku 4.5 for edits and Sonnet 5 batch for blueprints costs about ₹184.
tension: Every twelve-month scenario on Sonnet-for-everything loses money at ₹299.
Raising the price or cutting the caps both change what was already promised to the first users.

options.label: Split routing: Haiku for edits, Sonnet batch for blueprints
gains: Keeps ₹299.
About ₹60 margin a Pro user.
costs: Two models to maintain and monitor.
options.system: A routing rule per call type.
options.money: About ₹60 margin per Pro user a month.

options.label: Sonnet 5 for everything, price to ₹499 or more
gains: One model, simpler support.
costs: ₹200 higher than the plan promised.
options.money: Margin turns positive at the higher price.

options.label: Sonnet 5 for everything at ₹299, caps cut to 50 edits and 3 blueprints
gains: One model, simpler support.
costs: A visible downgrade to the free-to-Pro promise.

options.label: Keep ₹299, the caps and Sonnet, and absorb the loss
gains: Nothing changes for a user.
costs: About ₹120 lost per active Pro user a month.
options.money: About minus ₹120 per active Pro user a month.

recCase: Split routing is the only option that keeps every promise already made.
The margin is thin but positive, and caching is still unmeasured.
questions.flip: A week of real caching data showing Sonnet's cost after cache hits would reopen this.

questions.q: Does the free AI chain add a provider that trains on documents, or hold the line at four?
questions.lede: The sign-in page promises 'We never train on your documents'; one candidate provider's terms were never opened to check that.

visual.note: No OpenRouter endpoint until its terms are opened and quoted.
visual.caption: The free chain in fallback order, as the plan runs it today.

questions.stakes: The sign-in page's promise is only as true as the weakest provider in the fallback chain.
state: Groq, Cloudflare Workers AI and SambaNova's production models state no training in pages opened by research.
Cerebras is a 30-day trial behind a payment method.
OpenRouter's Nvidia-served endpoint carried an unverified training flag; its terms were never opened.
tension: About 260 active free users is where Cloudflare's free neurons run out and start costing money.
Adding a training-permitted provider means rewriting the sign-in promise, not just the chain.

options.label: Hold the chain at Groq, Cloudflare, Cerebras and SambaNova
gains: The sign-in promise stays true as written.
costs: Paid Cloudflare neurons from about 260 active free users.
options.money: Cloudflare overage from about 260 free users.

options.label: Add OpenRouter once its terms are opened and quoted with no training
gains: A wider free pool.
costs: Blocks on someone actually opening those terms.
options.money: Depends on the provider's own free tier.

options.label: Add a provider that trains, and change the sign-in promise
gains: A wider free pool immediately.
costs: The line becomes conditional: some providers may train.
options.money: Depends on the provider's own free tier.

recCase: This is the only option that needs nobody to check anything first.
The promise on the sign-in page stays literally true.
questions.flip: OpenRouter's terms being opened and read as no-training adds it back with no promise to rewrite.
sources: docs/mvp0/PRODUCT-PLAN.md, section 14, AI for the pilot

questions.q: Is frontmatter a markdown editor for the agent era, or the best markdown app in the world?
questions.lede: The plan took this sentence implicitly; the decision set reserved it for the founders to state.

rows.label: Customer group
cells: People whose documents are increasingly agent-written
Every note-taker, a much larger group

rows.label: Where Ideas sits
cells: Its own tab, ahead of the editor
Moves behind the editor, every phase

visual.caption: The sentence decides who the product is competing against.

questions.stakes: Every phase's build order, and the two competitors already named in the plan, follow from which sentence wins.
state: Revision 4 took K1 implicitly; the audit flagged it as reserved to the founders.
The plan's current sentence: a markdown editor for people whose documents are increasingly written with, and for, AI agents.
tension: The wider sentence reaches more people today, at the cost of the agent-era focus already built toward.
Changing K1 late moves Ideas in every phase, not just the home screen.

options.label: Keep the plan's sentence
gains: Matches everything already built and screened.
costs: A smaller starting customer group.

options.label: Adopt 'the best markdown note-taking app in the world'
gains: A much larger addressable group from day one.
costs: Ideas moves behind the editor in every phase.
options.screens: Every screen's ordering of Ideas changes.

options.label: Write a different sentence
gains: Fits a candidate not yet on the table.
costs: Every downstream section needs a fresh pass.

recCase: The plan, the screens and the research already argue for the agent-era sentence.
Nothing in the corpus argues the wider claim; adopting it would be asserted, not evidenced.
questions.flip: Twenty kit recipients naming general note-taking, not agent workflows, as their reason to stay would overturn this.

questions.q: Do we hold every cloud document from phase A, or carry the pilot on the desktop and hold only shared pages?
questions.lede: Card K2 said hold as little as possible for as little time as possible; sign-in-first with cloud documents on Free makes that hard to keep.

rows.label: Where phase F, the desktop app, sits
cells: After Drive sync, later in the sequence

rows.label: What the free caps mean before sync ships
Data held
cells: Every cloud document, from the first sign-in
Only what a person chooses to share

visual.caption: Sign-in first collides with holding as little as possible.

questions.stakes: This decides whether phase F, the desktop app, comes before or after phase A, the door.
state: The plan holds every document on R2 and Supabase from day one.
Card K2 recommended holding as little as possible, for as little time as possible.
Sign-in first and cloud documents on Free make holding from phase A close to unavoidable.
tension: A desktop-first pilot delays the free caps having any meaning until sync ships.
Holding from phase A needs the deletion, export and retention rules written before a stranger signs in.

options.label: Hold every cloud document from phase A, under stated retention rules
gains: The plan's build order stays as sequenced.
costs: More data held, sooner, than K2's own recommendation.
options.system: Deletion, export and retention rules ship with phase A.

options.label: Desktop carries the pilot; the web holds only shared pages until sync exists
gains: Matches K2's instinct to hold little, for a while.
costs: Phase F moves before phase A.
options.system: Sync becomes a phase-A dependency instead of phase F's.
options.screens: S25, desktop, moves earlier in the flow.

recCase: Sign-in first was already decided, and it makes minimal holding impractical.
The retention rules the audit asked for now exist in the data model section.
questions.flip: A founder deciding sign-in-first was itself the wrong call reopens this from the other end.

questions.q: Does live editing stay in phase D on the CRDT exception, or move to Later?
questions.lede: Yjs is a CRDT; the plan says never a CRDT and uses Yjs elsewhere, so the exception has to be written down, not assumed.

visual.note: Nothing from the session persists past the save.
visual.caption: The exception: session state never reaches disk.

questions.stakes: This is the one place the plan's own sync rule and its live-editing feature can look like they contradict each other.
state: Yjs is a CRDT by construction.
The exception: session state lives only while two people have the file open; every save is a splice.
Revision 3 carried this exception paragraph; revision 4 dropped it; revision 5 restores it.
tension: A CRDT ban with a live CRDT feature reads as a contradiction unless the exception is on the record.
Cutting live editing removes the only feature the three-collaborator cap actually measures live.

options.label: Keep live editing in phase D, on the written exception
gains: The three-collaborator cap keeps its live meaning.
costs: The exception has to hold under scrutiny.
options.system: No change; Yjs stays session-only, never persisted.

options.label: Cut live editing to Later
gains: No exception to defend.
costs: The three-collaborator cap becomes a sharing cap, not a live one.
options.system: Phase D loses its Yjs dependency, shrinks by about a week.
options.screens: S19, live collaboration, moves to Later.

recCase: The exception is real and narrow: nothing from the session ever reaches disk.
Cutting a shipped-feeling feature to defend a rule against a hypothetical reading costs more than keeping it.
questions.flip: A working session surviving a crash with state intact would mean Yjs is persisting something, and the exception would no longer hold.

questions.q: Are the free caps 50 documents, 5 pages and 3 collaborators, or the founders' original 5, 2 and 1?
questions.lede: A blueprint alone is fifteen files; the market floor across the forty pricing pages examined is 50 documents.

rows.label: One blueprint alone
cells: Blows past the cap on its own

visual.caption: The founders' original numbers do not fit one blueprint.

questions.stakes: A cap a single blueprint cannot fit inside blocks the idea funnel on day one, for every free user.
state: The market floor across forty pricing pages examined is 50 free documents; nobody caps public pages by count.
A blueprint is fifteen files by itself.
A downgraded account keeps every document readable and exportable, and cannot create new ones until under the cap.
tension: 5 documents blocks the import funnel and the idea funnel on day one.
50 is generous against the market floor, which argues the studio should say why, not just what.

options.label: 50 documents, 5 published pages, 3 live collaborators
gains: A blueprint fits inside the free cap.
Sits at the market floor, not below it.
costs: Higher than the founders' first candidates.
options.screens: S33, over cap, uses these numbers.

options.label: 5 documents, 2 published pages, 1 live collaborator
gains: Matches the founders' original candidates.
costs: Blocks the import and idea funnels on day one.
options.screens: S33 and the idea screens change their blocking point.

recCase: No blueprint can be tried at all under the founders' original numbers.
Fifty sits exactly at the floor forty pricing pages already set, not above it.
questions.flip: Evidence that free users at 50 documents never convert would argue for a tighter cap.

questions.q: Does the desktop app ship after Drive sync, or first, and who signs the Windows build?
questions.lede: Azure Artifact Signing excludes Indian entities; an Apple developer programme seat is 99 US dollars a year.

visual.caption: The Windows question is the same either way; only its timing changes.

questions.stakes: Shipping Windows unsigned trades a security warning on every install for skipping a certificate cost nobody has priced.
state: Azure Artifact Signing, Microsoft's own signing route, excludes Indian entities.
An Apple Developer Programme seat is 99 US dollars a year, and covers macOS signing.
A commercial Windows certificate has not been priced in this plan.
tension: Shipping first without a Windows answer forces the real decision mid-build instead of before it.
Waiting for Drive sync delays every desktop-only user by however long sync takes.

options.label: Ship after Drive sync, macOS signed, Windows shown as coming
gains: Follows the sequence already argued in the plan.
costs: A Windows user waits with no signed build.
options.money: A Windows certificate, priced before it is needed.

options.label: Ship the desktop app first, answer Windows before, not after
gains: Desktop-only users are not waiting on sync.
costs: A certificate decision is forced now, not later.
options.system: Phase F moves ahead of phase E.
options.screens: S25 moves earlier in the flow.

recCase: Nothing in the pace evidence argues for reordering the phases yet.
A Windows certificate is a cost to shop for, not to decide under pressure.
questions.flip: A pilot cohort skewed heavily toward desktop-only Windows users would argue for moving the phase and the certificate up.

questions.q: Does phase 0 return with twenty hand-made kits before phase C, or does Ideas ship on conviction?
questions.lede: An earlier revision gated everything on twenty hand-made kits; a later one dropped the gate without a record.

visual.note: The stop and continue lines in question 15 are read off this same funnel.
visual.caption: What happens to twenty hand-made kits, if the gate returns.

questions.stakes: Building on conviction instead of this funnel is exactly what the 13 September reset and the earlier revision both existed to stop.
state: An earlier plan gated Ideas on twenty hand-made kits for people outside the studio.
A later revision dropped the gate with no note explaining why.
Five of twenty running the kickoff prompt, two of ten editing the kit again, are the pass line.
tension: Twenty kits by hand is real founder time before any code for phase C is written.
Shipping on conviction risks repeating whatever made the studio reverse an earlier cut in the first place.

options.label: Phase 0 returns: twenty hand-made kits before phase C starts
gains: The gate that reversed an earlier cut is back in force.
costs: Founder time on kits instead of code.
options.screens: No change; phase C waits on this gate.

options.label: Ideas ships on conviction; the kill line moves to the pilot
gains: Phase C starts sooner.
costs: No outside-the-studio signal before building it.

recCase: This exact gate is why the generator and kickoff prompt exist in the plan at all.
Twenty kits by hand is a small cost against building Ideas on nothing but conviction.
questions.flip: A founder judging the earlier reversal to have been wrong reopens this from the root.
sources: docs/mvp0/PRODUCT-PLAN.md, section 26, the build in appetites

questions.q: Should a published page be indexed by search engines, kept out always, or switched on by its author?
questions.lede: The plan names no growth channel other than search, and the shipped code keeps every published page out of it.

visual.note: The last three are the three options, not a sequence.
visual.caption: Today's default, and the three ways to change it.

questions.stakes: This decides whether the product has a second growth channel beyond word of mouth, or has to name one.
state: robots.ts disallows /p/, so every published page is out of search today.
The plan names no growth channel other than search.
No default was carried into this revision; the audit raised it from the growth angle alone.
tension: Indexing by default trades a stranger's privacy expectation for a channel the plan currently lacks.
Staying unindexed means the plan still needs another answer to how anyone finds frontmatter.

options.label: Index published pages by default, with an unlisted switch
gains: A working growth channel from day one.
costs: A published page is public-by-default, not private-by-default.
options.system: robots.ts allows /p/; an unlisted flag per page.
options.screens: S17, share, gains a visibility toggle.

options.label: Never index; the plan names another channel
gains: A published page stays private unless shared directly.
costs: The plan still needs a real answer for growth.

options.label: Unlisted by default, indexed only when the author switches it on
gains: Privacy by default, a channel for whoever wants it.
costs: Most authors never find the switch.
options.screens: S17 gains a visibility toggle, off by default.

recCase: No other card in this set has to name a growth channel from scratch; this one does.
Unlisted by default costs no privacy and still lets an author opt into search.
questions.flip: A pilot with zero organic sign-ups by week four would argue for indexing by default instead.
sources: docs/mvp0/PRODUCT-PLAN.md, section 29, questions for the founders
